passage:
Saturday: At Rohit's birthday lunch, Rohit's grandmother handed Yash, fifteen, a steel plate and pointed him to the steps outside. Everyone else sat on the mats inside. "It's our custom," she said, not looking at him. Nobody said anything. Yash ate two bites, said he felt sick and walked home. He didn't tell his parents. He felt like dirt.
Monday: In class Yash didn't speak at all. At break, Aparna ma'am, the class teacher, asked him to help carry books and gently asked what was wrong. It came out in a rush. She put the books down. "Yash, what happened was wrong, and it is not your fault. You are not less than anyone." That afternoon she called Yash's parents and then Rohit's mother, and she reported it to the principal.
Wednesday: Rohit came to Yash's desk, red-faced. "Mummy says it was wrong. I'm sorry I didn't say anything." At lunch he sat beside Yash and they shared a tiffin.

qa.q: Where was Yash told to eat at Rohit's birthday lunch?
qa.a: On the steps outside, with a steel plate.

qa.q: How did Yash feel after being sent to eat on the steps?
qa.a: He felt deeply hurt and humiliated, like dirt, so ashamed he didn't even tell his parents.

qa.q: What did Aparna ma'am do that helped, and why?
qa.a: She named the exclusion as wrong, told Yash it was not his fault, and that same day called both families and reported it to the principal, acting to end it.

qa.q: How might Rohit have felt when he apologised?
qa.a: Rohit seemed ashamed and sorry, red-faced about staying silent, and wanting to show Yash he was on his side.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager made to eat separately because of caste custom, who feels less than others, and an adult who names the exclusion as wrong and acts.

subtype: Eating with friends of every kind [Actor]
passage:
Thursday, hostel, late
Irfan brought his mother's biryani back from Hyderabad today and offered me some. I'm vegetarian, he knows, so he'd kept a separate box of veg biryani just for me. That's the kind of friend he is. We ate on his bed with Marcus and Ramesh.
Then Mummy called. When I told her, she said, "Don't eat from the same boxes as those boys. And keep your own plate." I just said "okay" and hung up. I felt sick, and angry. Irfan had cooked for me, well, his mother had. What does "those boys" even mean?
Here's what I've decided. I'll stay vegetarian, because I actually believe in it. I'll respect Irfan not eating pork, which Ramesh keeps forgetting. But I'm not going to act like my friends are dirty. I'll talk to Mummy properly when I'm home at Diwali, not on the phone.
Chetan

qa.q: What did Irfan keep separately for Chetan?
qa.a: A separate box of veg biryani.

qa.q: How did Chetan feel after Mummy's phone call?
qa.a: Chetan felt sick and angry, because the call treated a caring friend as someone to keep apart from.

qa.q: How is Chetan balancing respect for food rules with fairness?
qa.a: Chetan keeps a chosen vegetarian diet and respects Irfan's no-pork rule, but refuses the unfair idea that friends are impure, planning to discuss it calmly at home.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel if he heard Mummy's words?
qa.a: Irfan would probably feel hurt and insulted, after making sure Chetan had a vegetarian box.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult in a hostel sharing meals across faiths and diets, respecting restrictions while questioning unfair purity ideas.

passage:
Coordinator's note, Sunday community lunch, Lane 4 hall.
This month Asif volunteered to host. His family's kitchen is halal, and he cooked his Ammi's mutton korma the way she taught him. But he also made a big pot of dal, jeera rice and a paneer dish, and labelled each one clearly: "Veg", "Halal meat", "No onion-garlic" for the Jain family from Block C. He even asked Mrs Shah beforehand what spices she avoids.
When a teenager joked loudly about someone's "grass plate", Asif laughed but said, "Everyone's plate is good here," and served the boy extra dal. The boy had seconds.
At the end, old Mr Pillai, who is strictly vegetarian, told me he had never felt so welcome at a lunch run by "meat people". Asif heard, smiled, and said, "Next month you teach me your avial." I'd like Asif on the organising team.
Farida, coordinator

qa.q: What did Asif write on the labels?
qa.a: "Veg", "Halal meat" and "No onion-garlic".

qa.q: How might Asif have felt when the teenager joked about the grass plate?
qa.a: He was probably a little uncomfortable but calm, answering lightly that everyone's plate is good here.

qa.q: What did Asif do that balanced tradition and respect?
qa.a: He kept his family's halal cooking, offered clearly labelled choices for vegetarian and Jain guests, and never let anyone's food be mocked.

qa.q: How did Mr Pillai experience the lunch?
qa.a: Mr Pillai felt unusually welcome, enjoying food he could eat and a host who respected his vegetarian diet.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who keeps his family's food custom yet offers guests a choice and never mocks anyone's plate.

passage:
Friday: Usha, twenty-four, stayed at her friend Bhavna's house in Rajkot. At dinner, Bhavna's mother dropped roti after roti on their plates, hot from the tawa. Bhavna covered her plate. "Mummy, enough!" Her mother's face fell. She turned back to the stove, stirring hard.
Saturday: The same thing. Usha watched her face each time Bhavna refused. It wasn't pride; it looked like hurt. She noticed how early aunty had woken to knead dough, how she asked what each of them liked.
Sunday: When aunty came with another roti, Usha smiled up at her. "Aunty, your rotis are softer than my mother's. I'll take half, with ghee, and then I'm truly full." Aunty glowed and tore one carefully. Bhavna watched, then said, "Mummy, half for me too. Thank you." Her mother touched Bhavna's hair on the way back to the stove.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do when her mother dropped more roti on Friday?
qa.a: She covered her plate and said, "Mummy, enough!"

qa.q: What did Usha feel as she watched Bhavna's mother on Saturday?
qa.a: Usha felt tender and thoughtful, realising the mother's face showed hurt, and that feeding was her way of showing love.

qa.q: What made Usha's response kind?
qa.a: She thanked aunty warmly, praised the rotis and took a little more before explaining she was full, which honoured the love behind the food.

qa.q: How does Bhavna's mother experience refusals of her roti?
qa.a: She feels them as rejection, turning away and stirring hard, because feeding is how she shows love.

grounding: It illustrates an observer who sees that a mother's extra rotis are her language of love and responds with thanks and warm explanation.

passage: On Christmas Eve in Kumasi, the house glowed with fairy lights. Kwame, two, stared at them, mouth open, and reached out to touch. Mama Yuki held him up. Then fireworks cracked outside. Kwame screamed and buried his face in her neck. She rocked him and hummed. Soon the aunties sang carols. Kwame peeked out, then bounced along.

qa.q: What did Kwame stare at?
qa.a: The fairy lights.

qa.q: How did Kwame feel when the fireworks cracked?
qa.a: He felt frightened, screaming and hiding his face in Mama Yuki's neck.

qa.q: What helped Kwame settle?
qa.a: Mama Yuki held and rocked him and hummed, and the aunties' singing made the house feel happy again.

qa.q: How might Mama Yuki feel when Kwame bounces along to the carols?
qa.a: She probably feels relieved and happy to see him enjoying the festival again.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler who reacts with wonder to festival lights and fear to loud noise, absorbing the mood of the house.

passage:
Preschool note, Diwali week.
Today the children made a rangoli at the entrance. I gave Yogesh the yellow powder and the job of filling the petals. He took it very seriously, tongue out, pinching the colour just as I showed him. When Harish stepped on a corner, Yogesh cried "Careful!" and fixed it himself. At home time he dragged his father to see it. "I made the yellow!" He asked me three times if we will make one again next year.

qa.q: What colour did Yogesh fill the petals with?
qa.a: Yellow.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel showing the rangoli to his father?
qa.a: He felt proud and excited, dragging his father to see it and announcing that he made the yellow.

qa.q: Why was giving Yogesh a real task a good idea?
qa.a: A real job made him feel part of the festival and the group, and gave him something to look forward to next year.

qa.q: How might Harish have felt when Yogesh shouted "Careful!"?
qa.a: Harish may have felt a bit startled or embarrassed at stepping on the corner.

grounding: It illustrates a child proud to have a real task in making a festival rangoli, giving him a place in the group.

passage: The power went out in the middle of the Holi story at the school assembly,. Himani's grandmother, who had come to tell it, kept going in the dark. "So Holika sat in the fire with little Prahlad on her lap, and the fire burned her, not him." Hafsa, nine, raised her hand though nobody could see it. "Why didn't it burn him?" "Because he was good and brave," Nani said. "Holi is about good winning." On the way home, Hafsa told Himani about Eid. "We give food to people who don't have any. Abbu says so everyone can be happy on the same day." Himani thought about it. "So both are about being good." That evening Hafsa asked Ammi if she could play Holi with Himani, and Ammi said yes.

qa.q: Who told the Holi story at the assembly?
qa.a: Himani's grandmother.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa ask why the fire didn't burn Prahlad?
qa.a: She was curious and puzzled by the story and wanted to understand its meaning.

qa.q: What did Hafsa take home from the day?
qa.a: A sense of both her own festival, Eid, and her friend's festival, Holi, with the idea that both are about being good.

qa.q: How might Himani's grandmother feel about Hafsa's question?
qa.a: She probably felt pleased that a child was listening closely enough to ask why, even in the dark.

grounding: It illustrates a child who hears a festival story, asks why, and takes home a sense of both her own and her friend's festival.

passage: Avni, you asked why I disappeared all Diwali week, so listen. I'm Preeti, sixteen, and in our house Diwali starts ten days early with cleaning. Every cupboard. Every fan. I was supposed to go to the movie with you all on Thursday, remember? Mummy said, "Movie? Who'll clean the kitchen shelves?" I sulked. I scrubbed those shelves like they'd insulted me. Then Friday we made chaklis with Nani, and she told stories about Diwali in her village, and I laughed so much I forgot I was angry. That's the confusing part. I hated the work and I loved being in it. So on Saturday I tried something new. I said, "Mummy, I'll do all the diyas and the rangoli, but can I have Sunday evening with my friends?" She looked surprised, then said yes. So Sunday, I'm yours, Avni.

qa.q: What did Preeti offer to do in exchange for Sunday evening?
qa.a: All the diyas and the rangoli.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel during Diwali week?
qa.a: Preeti felt resentful and grumpy about the cleaning, but also happy and close to family while making chaklis with Nani.

qa.q: What worked about Preeti's request on Saturday?
qa.a: She offered to share some festival duty and calmly asked for specific personal time, which made it easy for Mummy to say yes.

qa.q: How might Avni have felt when Preeti disappeared all week?
qa.a: Avni was probably a bit disappointed and confused about the missed movie, and pleased to hear Preeti had kept Sunday for friends.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager pulled into festival duties while wanting time with friends, who feels both grumbling and belonging and asks for personal time.

passage:
Dear Varun,
It's Diwali week in our colony again, and it's strange without you. You know how it was before you moved: every balcony full of lights, crackers, sweet boxes going door to door, and our flat dark. We're Tibetan; Losar is in February, and nobody here has heard of it. For years I sat inside with the curtains shut, feeling like we lived in a different country.
Then you knocked, three Diwalis ago, and dragged me down to light diyas with your family. Your mother gave me kaju katli and said, "Next year, you bring something from your festival." I still remember how warm that felt.
This year, guess what. Mrs Rao from 3B knocked. "Tenzin, come for Lakshmi puja. Bring your mother." We went. My mother brought khapse, our Losar biscuits. Everyone ate them all.
I'm inviting the whole floor for Losar. You're invited too, even from Pune.
Tenzin

qa.q: What did Tenzin's mother bring to the Lakshmi puja?
qa.a: Khapse, their Losar biscuits.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel during Diwali before Varun's invitation?
qa.a: Tenzin felt left out and lonely, sitting inside with the curtains shut as if living in a different country.

qa.q: What does Tenzin's story show about invitations?
qa.a: A simple invitation from a friend or neighbour costs little but can make someone from a minority family feel part of the community.

qa.q: How might Mrs Rao have felt when everyone ate the khapse?
qa.a: She probably felt glad and warm, happy that her invitation brought Tenzin's family and their festival into the colony.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager from a minority migrant family who feels outside neighbours' festivals, and how invitations make a big difference.

passage:
On Bohag Bihu, Ritu, nineteen, sat in her Pune hostel room watching her cousins' videos from Jorhat: the dhol, the mekhela sadors, her aunt making pitha on the fire. Her chest ached. She hadn't known a festival could hurt from far away. Her roommate Anjali found her with swollen eyes. "Is everything okay?" Ritu shook her head. "It's Bihu. Everyone's home except me."
Anjali sat down. "What do you eat on Bihu?" "Pitha. Rice cakes, with jaggery and sesame." "Do we have rice flour?" They didn't, but the shop downstairs did. At midnight the two of them burnt the first batch on Anjali's hot plate and laughed until they cried. Ritu video-called her Ma, holding up a wonky pitha. Ma laughed too. The next day, Anjali found an Assamese students' group meeting on Sunday. Ritu still missed home. But she went.

qa.q: What did Ritu and Anjali make on the hot plate?
qa.a: Pitha, rice cakes with jaggery and sesame.

qa.q: How was Ritu feeling while watching her cousins' videos?
qa.a: She felt a sharp ache of homesickness, missing her family at Bihu.

qa.q: Which small steps eased Ritu's homesickness?
qa.a: Cooking pitha with Anjali, video-calling Ma and going to the Assamese students' group, which eased the ache without pretending it was small.

qa.q: How might Ritu's Ma have felt seeing the wonky pitha on the call?
qa.a: Ma probably felt amused and moved, glad her daughter was celebrating even far from home.

grounding: It illustrates a student far from home who aches during a festival and eases it by calling home, cooking one dish and joining a local group.
